To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we identified putative regulatory regions for HPS genes using phylogenetic footprint analysis and verified them using in vitro transcription assays; (2) we identified putatively shared transcription factor binding sites among the three HPS genes; (3) we identified a mutation in a putative promoter region of HPS3 in a patient with decreased HPS3 RNA and no mutation in the coding regions.

phylogenetic footprint analysis identified conserved regions in HPS3, 5, and 6 that were verified to have transcriptional activation activity in luciferase assays, and the HPS3 consvred region was sequenced to identify potential regulatory elements in patients with low levels of fibroblast HPLS RNA.
phylogenetic footprint analysis of HPS3 and HPS5 identified putative promoter elements, and that the upstream sequence of HPS3 is mutated in patients with HPS3 RNA but not HPS3 protein deficiency.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the promoter elements of the HPS genes.
the identification of the promoter regions of the three HPS genes HPS3, 5, and 6, which are members of the Biogenesis of Lymphosome-Related Organelles Complex-2 (BLOC-2).
the identification and characterization of the promoter elements for three of the eight human HPS genes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
phylogenetic footprint analysis of the HPS3 promoter identified conserved elements in the promoter region of the human HPS3 gene.
phylogenetic footprint analysis is a useful method in the identification of potential regulatory regions for the HPS genes.
the conserved regions of the HPS3 gene are likely to be involved in the regulation of gene expression.

phylogenetic footprint analysis is an effective method for identifying putative promoter elements in non-coding regions.
